Industry observers note that we found that targeting the AMOTL2 TSS led to a complete knockdown of AMOTL2 expression in HCASMCs and human coronary artery endothelial cells (HCAECs) (Fig. 5c). Importantly, targeting the rs9876658-containing enhancer reduced AMOTL2 expression in HCASMCs but not HCAECs, bolstering our prediction (Fig. 5c). Collectively, these analyses nominate rs9876658 as a causal regulator of AMOTL2 expression in SMCs but not endothelial cells and implicate this gene as a new candidate gene for atherosclerosis through an effect in SMCs. To dissect the functional impact of targeting AMOTL2 in HCASMCs, we compared non-targeting control and AMOTL2 knockdown HCASMCs. We observed disordered cellular morphology as well as decreased calponin (CNN1) and alpha-smooth muscle actin (ACTA2) expression by immunofluorescence in AMOTL2 knockdown cells, suggesting a shift away from the quiescent contractile state (Fig. 5d). We performed bulk RNA sequencing in stressed non-targeting control and AMOTL2 knockdown cells (Fig. 5e). Gene ontology pathway analysis revealed an upregulation of cell-cycle-related genes and a downregulation of cell-motility-associated pathways (Fig. 5f). Consistent with our immunofluorescence staining (Fig. 5d), we saw a reduction in contractile SMC gene expression (ACTA2, CNN1, TAGLN and LMOD1) in AMOTL2 knockdown cells relative to control (Fig. 5g). Finally, AMOTL2 knockdown cells had a significantly greater proliferation rate (Fig. 5h). Taken together, these findings establish a functional role for AMOTL2 in SMC proliferation and migration—pathways integral in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis.

Industry observers note that although GWAS have identified hundreds of CAD-associated variants1,5,28,29, translation to therapies remains limited by incomplete understanding of the causal cell types and gene programmes30,31. The emergence of multi-omic single-cell technologies has created a unique opportunity to profile human tissue at unprecedented resolution14,32. Numerous studies have leveraged these technologies to uncover cellular heterogeneity in human tissue across many diseases, contributing to a human cell atlas17,18,24,33. Few studies have mapped common disease variants to causal cell types and target genes directly in human tissue, with previous work limited by unimodal profiling or cell-based systems that lack the native tissue context.

In a recent development, our study used a newly introduced technique—single-nucleus multi-ome (RNA+ATAC)—in human coronary arteries from 44 patients with paired genotyping for unbiased characterization of the transcriptome and epigenome at single-cell resolution. Capturing paired gene expression and chromatin accessibility from the same nucleus allows for more robust peak-gene linkage21 and represents an important milestone for regulatory biology of the human vasculature. We also used a new computational framework—scE2G21—to build an unbiased genome-wide scE2G map in human CAD. Notably, our scV2E2G framework identified a substantial set of CAD-associated enhancer–gene links in SMCs, including 325 linked genes, providing a basis for downstream functional interrogation of SMC regulatory programmes. This systematic approach can be applied broadly across diseases and allows for an unbiased framework to prioritize pathological genes and cell types driving common heritable human diseases.

To nominate functional regulatory variants in a broader cohort, we integrated our data with published human coronary artery snATAC–seq19 to identify 11,269 sc-caQTLs, enabling QTL discovery in cell types that are obscured in bulk analyses34,35. Mechanistic dissection of rs658956 illustrates how non-coding CAD variants can act through cell-type-specific disruption of transcription factor binding and enhancer activity36. The disruption of an AP-1 (JUN/FOS) motif by this variant is particularly notable given the well-established role of AP-1 in SMC phenotypic switching and the recent evidence that AP-1 family members act as pioneer factors governing vascular cell chromatin landscapes37 and carry epigenetic memory of inflammation38. Furthermore, SMC-specific regulation of the lncRNA FGGY-DT highlights the potential contribution of cell-restricted non-coding RNA programmes to cardiovascular disease39,40,41, although its downstream role remains to be defined.

Recent findings suggest that traditional pseudobulk QTL discovery lacks the ability to discriminate between molecular traits that are influenced by disease state3. Here we used single-cell genomics to define cell-state dynamics in one of the most fluid cell types in the atherosclerotic plaque. In atherosclerosis, contractile SMCs undergo de-differentiation and acquire an FMC phenotype with distinct transcriptional signatures16. We applied a continuous score reflecting SMC to FMC transition to map dynamic caQTLs that are dependent on cell-state. Using this framework, we uncovered rs658956 as a caQTL for FGGY-DT enhancer that is associated with altered activity as SMCs transition to FMCs. This is an application of single-cell-state-dependent QTL modelling in human cardiovascular disease and expands our understanding of gene regulation in heterogeneous cell states.

We applied arrayed Perturb–seq42 to GWAS-nominated enhancers and their SMC-linked target genes, enabling transcriptome-wide functional validation of non-coding regulatory elements and their downstream gene programmes. Critically, the arrayed format preserves non-cell-autonomous transcriptional effects that can be obscured in pooled screens where shared culture conditions confound intrinsic regulatory responses through paracrine signalling, as in a recent CAD variant-to-gene-to-programme framework26. The convergence of several enhancer perturbations on inflammatory and ECM-remodelling programmes is consistent with the established role of stated processes in atherosclerosis, including induction of matrix metalloproteinases and collagens43. Together, these data support a model in which CAD variants act through cell-type-specific enhancers to co-ordinately dysregulate inflammation, ECM homeostasis and proliferation during transition from contractile SMCs to pathological FMCs18,44.

Given that the genome is organized as a dynamic 3D structure45, chromatin looping through topologically associating domains (TADs) represents a higher-order regulatory layer governing gene expression45,46. Although Hi-C has been used in cell-based systems and other tissues to map chromatin architecture and connect disease variants to distal genes47,48, large-scale chromatin structures are highly tissue- and cell-type-specific27,48,49 and remain unexplored in diseased human arterial tissue. Here, genome-wide Hi-C in 15 human coronary arteries enabled tissue-specific mapping of chromatin networks and distal variant–gene interactions. Notably, we discovered that rs4887091 creates an allele-specific CTCF binding site with dosage-dependent effects on both CTCF occupancy and loop strength, defining a mechanistically distinct non-coding regulatory mechanism involving 3D genome architecture48. Haplotype-resolved analysis confirmed the allele-specific increase in looping strength50,51, consistent with recent demonstrations that phased Hi-C can resolve allele-specific chromatin structure at disease loci52 and that variants within CTCF sites can alter looping and gene regulation in a dosage-sensitive manner50,51. The linked gene, ADAMTS7, is causally implicated in CAD, with Adamts7 deficiency reducing atherosclerosis and its catalytic activity regulating SMC migration53,54. Although our data do not establish altered looping as the proximal mechanism controlling ADAMTS7 expression, allele-dependent changes to chromatin architecture may represent a previously unrecognized regulatory mechanism at this locus.

Recent findings suggest that furthermore, our tissue Hi-C framework enabled systematic genome-wide nomination of distal causal genes. We identified 11 genes linked to CAD variants through chromatin contacts, most of which, for example AMOTL2, were not the gene nearest to the disease-associated variant. CRISPRi targeting of the enhancer linked distally to AMOTL2 reduced AMOTL2 expression in HCASMCs but not HCAECs, and AMOTL2 knockdown in HCASMCs increased cellular proliferation and suppressed contractile marker expression, consistent with a shift away from a quiescent state. This phenotype aligns with the known function of AMOTL2 as a scaffold protein55,56 that retains YAP in the cytoplasm to suppress Hippo-driven proliferative transcription, such that its loss de-represses YAP nuclear activity and promotes cell-cycle progression57. The connection between a CAD-associated variant and a Hippo pathway regulator with established roles in vascular cell proliferation and mechanosensing58,59 points to dysregulation of YAP and/or TAZ signalling in SMCs as a potentially underappreciated axis in atherosclerotic disease.

Sources indicate that our study has several limitations. First, nuclear RNA provides more limited cell-state resolution than whole-cell RNA, so we leveraged high-resolution published single-cell data for reference mapping and state imputation. Second, caQTL discovery remains constrained by sample size, cell abundance and allele frequency, limiting power in rarer cell types and variants and complicating interpretation of differences in caQTLs across cell types. Residual population stratification in our multi-ancestry cohort may have also resulted in false positives, although our summary statistics can support future meta-analyses in larger cohorts. Third, multi-ome profiling does not capture post-transcriptional regulation such as alternative splicing. Finally, bulk coronary Hi-C precludes genome-wide cell-type-specific looping inference; we therefore used targeted Hi-ChIP–seq for cell-type resolution at selected loci. Although CRISPRi Perturb–seq supports ADAMTS7 as a responsive target of the rs4887091-containing enhancer, direct allele editing or CTCF motif perturbation will be required to establish whether allele-dependent looping causally regulates ADAMTS7 expression.

According to recent reports, in conclusion, we built a multi-omic gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility map of human CAD and provide a comprehensive framework to map CAD GWAS variants to causal genes and affected cell types. Furthermore, we use pseudobulk and single-cell QTL modelling to characterize state-dependent and independent regulatory mechanism of disease variants in human tissue. We used tissue Hi-C to build large-scale chromatin networks and uncover how disease variants impact distal gene regulation. Finally, we integrated tissue -omics with in vitro epigenetic profiling to prioritize and functionally test candidate genes using Perturb–seq and CRISPRi. Collectively, we provide a disease agnostic framework to apply human genetic findings to nominate pathologic cell states and genes driving disease, constructing a comprehensive GWAS variant-to-gene map with genetic- and tissue-level convergence for future mechanistic and therapeutic studies.

The study is compliant with all relevant ethical regulations and has been approved by the Washington University School of Medicine Institutional Review Board (no. 201104172). Informed consent was obtained from each patient before tissue collection by Washington University School of Medicine; no compensation was provided in exchange for participation in the study, and participants consented to publication of research data. Written consent was obtained. Demographic data have been de-identified and are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Patients included in this study span diverse race, age and sex to provide an inclusive trans-ethnic study population.

Before tissue collection, specific inclusion criteria were used to ensure well controlled study groups. Any patients with human immunodeficiency virus or hepatitis and known genetic cardiomyopathies were excluded from this study. The left anterior descending coronary artery was isolated, and flash frozen from donor hearts (patients with stable ejection fractions who experienced non-cardiac cause of death) and from patients with chronic heart failure (ischaemic and non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy) at the time of heart transplantation. For all samples, the proximal left anterior descending coronary artery was used. All demographic and clinical data have been de-identified and are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Recruitment was therefore determined by donor and/or transplant tissue availability and clinical indication rather than population-based sampling, which may limit generalizability to the broader CAD population.

Sources indicate that the left anterior descending coronary artery was dissected from explanted hearts; epicardial fat was removed, and arteries were flash frozen using liquid nitrogen. Identical regions from the proximal left anterior descending artery were used from all patients. Single-nuclei suspensions were generated as described previously17. Nuclei were isolated according to the 10x Genomics protocol (Nuclei Isolation Complex Sample for ATAC GEX Sequencing RevB, CG000375) and flow cytometry for 7-AAD (Sigma, SML1633-1ML) positive nuclei was used for sorting using a BD FACS Melody (BD Biosciences) with a 100-µm nozzle. Protocol CG000338 from 10x Genomics was used for Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multi-ome ATAC + Gene Expression. Briefly, following nuclei isolation, permeabilization was performed, followed by transposition, GEM generation and barcoding using ChipJ (10x Genomics, PN1000234), post-GEM clean up, pre-amplification PCR, cDNA amplification, library construction and sequencing. Gene-expression and ATAC libraries were sequenced to a read depth of 50,000 and 25,000, respectively, using a NovaSeq 6000 platform (Illumina) at the McDonnell Genome Institute. Data were acquired and sorted using BD FACSChorus v.1.1.

Raw fastq files were aligned to the human GRCh38 reference genome using CellRanger ARC (10x Genomics, v.6.1), with ATAC data processed in ArchR (v.1.0.3)60 and RNA data in Seurat (v.5.5.1). After quality control, doublet removal, SCTransform normalization (sctransform v.0.4.3)61, Harmony integration (v.2.0.5)62, clustering and RNA-based cell-type annotation, RNA annotations were transferred to the paired ATAC profiles. Detailed quality control thresholds and clustering procedures are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1.

Industry observers note that we used the scE2GMulti-ome model21 to predict enhancer–gene connections in 11 cell types from 10x Genomics multi-ome data. In each cell type, scE2G scores every candidate element–gene pair (where candidate elements are ATAC peaks within 5 Mb of the TSS of the gene) by integrating several features. Regulatory enhancer–gene interactions were defined as element–gene pairs with a score greater than 0.171.

The scE2Gmulti-ome model is a supervised classifier adapted for multi-omic data from ENCODE-rE2G63. It integrates eight features, including (1) a pseudobulk activity-by-contact score, where 3D contact is estimated by an inverse function of genomic distance; (2) the Kendall correlation across single cells between element accessibility and gene expression; (3) whether the gene is ‘expressed ubiquitously’ and (4) several other measures of genomic distance and chromatin accessibility around the element and promoter. The score threshold of 0.171 was determined as the score yielding 70% recall when evaluating predictions in K562 cells against CRISPRi-validated enhancer–gene pairs.

scE2G predictions for all cell types can be found in Supplementary Tables 3–14. To construct the disease-relevant scV2E2G map, we selected ATAC–seq peaks from the four main cell types that contained a CAD GWAS variant, defined cell-type-specific enhancers by overlap with coronary artery H3K27ac peaks, linked these enhancers to genes using scE2G and finally overlapped scE2G peaks with sc-caQTLs to nominate links supported by a molecular trait.

Recent findings suggest that to test for enrichment of disease risk in the four main cell types, stratified LDSC64 was used to partition heritability in cell-type marker peaks. First, cell-type specific marker peaks (FDR < 0.01, log2[fold change] > 1) were obtained using ArchR (v.1.0.3) and converted to GRCh37 coordinates using liftover65. GWAS summary statistics for CAD1, diabetes66, abdominal aortic aneurysms67, DBP and SBP68, and stroke 69 were obtained, and their formats were standardized using MungeSumstats (v.1.20.0)70. Stratified LD score analysis (LDSC v.1.0.1) was then carried out with --h2-cts flag for cell-type specific analyses. P values obtained from stratified LDSC were considered significant for a condition if they were lower than Bonferroni-corrected P value threshold of 8.33 × 10−3 (for six conditions tested). To examine overlap between CAD GWAS variants and ATAC peaks, lead variants from 241 genome-wide significant (P < 5 × 10−8) loci and 897 conditionally independent variants meeting FDR cutoff (FDR < 0.01) were obtained from Aragam and colleagues1. Additional variants that are in high linkage disequilibrium (r2 > 0.80 within 250 kb) with these lead variants were obtained from the 1000 Genomes European panel using PLINK v.1.9 --tag-r2 flag. Furthermore, these variants were combined with the functional fine-mapped credible set variants from Aragam and colleagues1 to create a superset of GWAS variants to be tested for overlap. These variants were overlapped with ATAC peak regions using the findOverlaps function in the IRanges R package (v.2.46.0).

Recent findings suggest that to obtain high-quality genotypes from patients, DNA from peripheral leukocytes of 39 participants was genotyped using Illumina GSA-24-V3 SNP array. Following initial processing using Illumina GenomeStudio software v.2.0.5, variants with both (1) minor allele frequency (MAF) >5% and call rate <95% or (2) MAF <5% and call rate <99% were excluded. No patients were excluded by the call rate exclusion filter (<95%). Additional genotypes were further imputed from the TOPMED panel on the Michigan Imputation Server v.1.7.1 using minimac v.4-1.0.2 (ref. 71) and phasing with Eagle v.2.4.1 (ref. 72). Following imputation, variants with imputation R2 > 0.3 and MAF > 0.05 were further kept for caQTL analysis for a final dataset containing 7,250,405 variants. To conduct combined caQTL mapping, the variant call format (VCF) files from Turner and colleagues19 were merged with the imputed genotype dataset, and shared SNPs in only two datasets were kept for downstream analysis. Turner and colleagues carried out low-coverage whole-genome sequencing; further details are available in the original publication19. Following the merge, 5,229,397 variants were available for QTL analysis. Local ancestries were inferred using RFMix v.2.03-r0 with default settings73. Yoruba in Ibadan, Nigeria (YRI, n = 186) and Utah residents with ancestry from northern and western Europe (CEU, n = 183) from the 1000 Genomes Project74 were used as African and/or European reference populations, respectively.

To achieve uniform cell-type annotations across datasets, snATAC–seq data from Turner and colleagues19 were reference mapped onto the multi-ome dataset rather than integrated. Raw snATAC–seq data from Turner and colleagues were downloaded and reprocessed using identical quality control thresholds (minimum fragment count and TSS enrichment cut-offs) as applied to the multi-ome snATAC–seq, ensuring consistent data processing upstream of annotation. Gene activity scores were computed from the snATAC–seq data from Turner and colleagues using ArchR (v.1.0.3)60 and used as the query, with the snRNA-seq component of the multi-ome data serving as the reference for label transfer through Seurat’s anchor-based framework (v.5.5.1). This approach leveraged the higher-quality transcriptomic annotations from the multi-ome dataset to annotate the external snATAC–seq data without merging the two datasets. Annotation concordance between transferred labels and author-provided annotations from Turner and colleagues19 was assessed using Jaccard Index across the four main cell populations used for QTL mapping.

Similar to previous studies for sc-caQTL discovery19,75, we used RASQUAL76 to identify pseudobulk caQTLs in four main cell types (SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts). RASQUAL v.1.1 was chosen as our mapping method due to its ability to simultaneously model allelic imbalance and count-based QTL effect to improve fine-mapping of putative causal variants. RASQUAL maximizes power for caQTL discovery by simultaneously modelling allelic imbalance and total read counts in each locus. To generate fragment counts within each ATAC peak regions, we loaded each fragment object and used Signac (v.1.17.1) FeatureMatrix function to generate a cell-by-peak count matrix for all cells within each cell type. This matrix was subsequently aggregated at a sample pseudobulk level using rollup function from the R slam package (v.0.1-56). For RASQUAL’s allele-specific modelling, createASVCF.sh script in paired-read mode was used to generate allele-specific fragment counts at each site with additional BAM flag of -F 1280 to exclude secondary or PCR duplicate reads. For each cell type, only samples with at least 20 cells of that cell type and only peaks with at least five reads on average across all samples were included for the final analysis.

In a recent development, for the caQTL association analysis, all variants within a ±10-kb cis-window of the peaks were tested for association. Total library size for each sample was included as an offset. Age, sex, sequencing site and first four principal components of genotype data (generated from plink --pca) were included as covariates. For multiple testing correction, we used the two-step correction procedure recommended by RASQUAL76, including locus-level correction followed by a genome-wide correction using an empirical null distribution generated using genotype permutations. The caQTL variants were queried subsequently in bulk eQTL datasets using Qtlizer (v.1.22.0)77. Power, MAF-stratified validation, model comparison and genotype-PC sensitivity analyses are described in Supplementary Fig. 2. For locus-level multiple testing, a Q value corresponding to SNP-level FDR was calculated using the Benjamini–Hochberg method, and the SNP with the lowest Q value was selected for each locus. For genome-wide correction, an empirical null distribution was calculated from four RASQUAL runs using randomly permuted genotypes; the averaged null distribution was used to obtain Q value cut-offs corresponding to 1%, 5% and 10% genome-wide FDR.

We compared the myeloid cell caQTLs with previously published monocyte caQTLs discovered in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 15 healthy donors. We found that 26.7% (767 of 2,868) of the lead macrophage caQTL variants were also the lead variant among the previously identified 3,528 monocyte caQTLs. Although only a minority, this difference may reflect the profoundly distinct biological environments between peripheral blood mononuclear cells and myeloid cells in atherosclerotic lesions75.

Pseudobulk caQTLs for the main cell types can be found in Supplementary Tables 15–26. To assess transcription factor binding potential at caQTLs, we trained seq2PRINT22 in SMCs using chromatin accessibility and ATAC footprinting to predict transcription factor binding probability at base-pair resolution and compared caQTL variants with non-caQTL cis-SNPs within accessible peaks.

In a recent development, by mapping our multi-ome dataset onto a recently published coronary artery CITE-seq dataset18, we demonstrated concordant mapping scores across SMC cell states, and projecting the FMC module score into this independent dataset confirmed the score was most enriched in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 5b–d). In human spatial transcriptomics data, the FMC score demonstrated greater enrichment in diseased relative to healthy coronary vessels (Extended Data Fig. 5e), and in carotid plaques the FMC score correlated positively with percent stenosis (Spearman ρ = 0.58, P = 0.019), linking FMC identity directly to disease burden (Extended Data Fig. 5f). Pseudotime trajectory analysis demonstrated progressive enrichment of the FMC score as SMCs differentiate, recapitulated by both our module and an independently published gene set (Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). Using an in vitro serum starvation and replenishment model of phenotypic switching in HCASMCs followed by scRNA-seq, we confirmed that the FMC score is elevated significantly in the stressed state (Extended Data Fig. 5i). Consistent with this, published time-course murine atherosclerosis data in SMC lineage-traced cells found progressive expansion of the FMC module with disease progression (Extended Data Fig. 5j). Finally, the FMC score was correlated positively with ChromVAR-predicted activity78 of established FMC transcriptional regulators including the MEF2 family, linking chromatin remodelling to transcriptional dynamics along this differentiation axis (Extended Data Fig. 5k). Collectively, these analyses establish the reproducibility of the FMC module across independent human datasets, its association with clinical disease burden, and its relevance to both in vitro and in vivo models of SMC phenotypic switching.

In a recent development, in addition to the pseudobulk caQTL model, we used a PME single-cell model to map caQTLs in SMCs. This approach models cell-level fragment counts with random effect covariates to account for relatedness shared by cells from the same sample and batch. Such attempts to model discrete count distributions at a single-cell level have been shown to generally boost power in single-cell QTL discovery compared with pseudobulk and/or linear regression frameworks79,80,81. Our PME model was adapted from the PME model used by Nathan and colleagues3 for single-cell eQTL mapping as follows:.

In a recent development, where ATAC fragment counts (A) was modelled with fixed-effect covariates (G, genotype; nFrags, number of fragments per cell, TSSEnrich, TSS enrichment per cell; accPC, principal components of single-nucleus ATAC counts; genoPC, principal components of genotype data), random effect covariates (d, donor ID; s, sequencing site) and intercept (θ). All quantitative covariates were scaled and centred before the regression analysis. Significance of the genotype effect term (βG) was tested by LRT of the full model containing the genotype term and a null model without the genotype term. Due to the high computational load of running Poisson regression analysis on all cells, this analysis was restricted to lead caQTL variants from the pseudobulk RASQUAL analysis, which models the fragment counts using a negative binomial model. All Poisson models were fit using the glmer function from the lme4 R package (v.2.0-6). We confirmed that our data is generally not over-dispersed by plotting the mean variance relationship between a random subset of peaks. Similarly, using a zero-inflated Poisson regression model or a negative binomial model on a subset of our hits revealed little differences in overall regression estimates. Given that a small proportion of our pseudobulk hits probably represent null results, we did not conduct FDR correction due to our inability to accurately estimate the proportion of results from the null distribution. Instead, we compared z values between our pseudobulk and PME models.

A key benefit of modelling individual cells instead of sample-level pseudobulk is our ability to simultaneously model cell-state covariates (for example, differentiation trajectories, gene and/or protein expression) as well as potential interaction between genotypes and cell-state covariates. We defined FMC identity score by calculating the gene activity of the top 100 FMC (modulated SMC) marker genes defined by Wirka and colleagues16 from our integrated snATAC–seq meta-map using ArchR (v.1.0.3) addGeneScoreMatrix() and Seurat (v.5.5.1) AddModuleScore(). To test for ‘dynamic’ caQTL where the genotype effect is modified by SMC cell state, we then added the FMC score and a genotype-FMC score interaction term as covariates in the following model:.

Again, this analysis was carried out just on the significant (FDR < 5%) lead variants from the pseudobulk caQTL analyses, although it is entirely possible that there are non-significant pseudobulk caQTLs (that is, genotype effect is near zero for average FMC score) that may have significant interaction terms. We obtained P values for the genotype-FMC score interaction term using an LRT. We subsequently applied Storey Q value correction to LRT P values of the interaction term across all tested variants for multiple-testing correction. Dynamic caQTLs can be found in Supplementary Tables 29 and 30.

For EMSA, reference allele probe (5′-atagttcagaaacctgactcagccccttctt-3′) and alternate allele probe (5′- atagttcagaaaccttactcagccccttctt-3′) for rs658956 were synthesized and labelled with IRDye700 (Integrated DNA Technologies). The labelled (100 nM) and competitor (5 μM) probes were incubated with 5–10 μg of SMC nuclear extract in binding buffer (final concentration 8% Ficoll, 160 mM KCl, 20 mM HEPES, 10 mM MgCl2, 2.5 mM dithiothreitol, 0.25% Tween-20) and 1 μg of Poly dI*dC competitor at 4 °C for 1 h. For supershift assays, the protein complex was also incubated with anti-cJun (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-74543), anti-cFos (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-166940) or anti-JunB (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-8051) before addition of the probe. Following incubation, the reaction mixture was run on a 5% TBE native gel in 4 °C for 30 min to 1 h. The gel was subsequently imaged using a Bio-Rad ChemiDoc Gel Imager.

Recent findings suggest that the most effective gRNA sequence targeting an enhancer was cloned individually into the pBA904 vector and transfected into CRISPRi-HCASMC. After 5 days, RNA was collected, extracted and converted to cDNA. The effect of enhancer targeting was then assessed by comparing the expression levels of the target genes LOXL1, MYO9B, NAV1 and PALLD with that of the control. RNA was isolated using RNeasy plus micro kit (Qiagen, 74034) and total cDNA was prepared using High-capacity RNA-to-cDNA kit (Life Technologies, 4388950).

Sources indicate that parental and dCas9-Zim3 SMCs were cultured for 3 days in full medium (SmGM-2 Smooth Muscle Cell Growth Medium; Lonza, CC-3182) followed by 3 days serum starvation (base medium only) and 3 days recovery with full medium. dCas9-Zim3 SMCs were also cultured under two additional conditions for profiling: (1) 3 days full medium and (2) 3 days full medium followed by 3 days serum starvation. Cells were then processed using the Single Cell 3′ v.4 OCM kit (10x Genomics, PN-1000779) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The library was sequenced on an Illumina Nextseq2000 with read lengths (Read 1: 28, Read 2: 90, Index 1: 10, Index 2: 10). Sequencing data were demultiplexed and aligned to the human genome (GRCh38-2024-A from 10x Genomics) using CellRanger (v.9.0.1).

Industry observers note that library preparation was conducted with Chromium GEM-X Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits v.4 (10x Genomics). Libraries were sequenced on NovaSeq X Plus. The initial 10x scRNA-seq dataset was processed using the CellRanger pipeline (v.8.0.0). The workflow included demultiplexing the bcl files with CellRanger mkfastq, followed by running CellRanger count using the pre-built CellRanger reference GRCh38-2020-A from 10x Genomics.

Sources indicate that lentivirus carrying gRNAs were produced by VectorBuilder by modifying a CROPseq vector to include a T7–U6 hybrid promoter as described previously82. Four guides were designed per TSS, three guides per enhancer region and two non-targeting controls. gRNA lentiviruses were pooled for each enhancer or TSS at a 1:1 ratio based on titre for knockdown. Cells were transfected at a multiplicity of infection of 5 and left to recover for 3 days. Puromycin (0.5 μg ml−1) was used to select for transfected cells for 4 days. Cells then underwent the 3-day starvation and 3-day recovery period as described above during which growth was monitored in an Incucyte S3 incubator and images analysed using Incucyte 2020B software. Cells were then used for single-cell transcriptomic analysis as described below.

According to recent reports, A total of 100,000 cells from each condition were fixed with the Low Input Cell Fixation v.3 kit (Parse Biosciences, ECLC3303) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were processed with the Evercode WT v.3 kit (Parse Biosciences, ECWT3300). Eight sub-libraries of 12,500 cells were generated according to manufacturer’s instructions and sequenced on an Illumina Nextseq2000 with read lengths (Read 1, 64; Read 2, 58; Index 1: 8; Index 2, 8). Sequencing data were demultiplexed and aligned to the human genome (GRCh38 Parse Biosciences) using split-pipe (v.1.6.3).

Raw count matrices generated by Parse Biosciences split-pipe demultiplexing were imported into R using the ReadMtx function from Seurat v.4, loading the count matrix, cell metadata and gene annotation files from the DGE_filtered directory. A Seurat object was created requiring genes detected in at least three cells and a minimum of 200 features per cell. Mitochondrial content was calculated using PercentageFeatureSet. Cells were filtered to retain those with 200–7,500 detected genes and less than 25% mitochondrial reads. Untransduced cells and two genomic coordinate-labelled perturbation conditions were excluded. Perturbation identities were mapped from sample barcodes to gene or enhancer labels, and cells were classified as non-targeting or perturbed. Gene-expression data were normalized using Seurat NormalizeData, variable features identified with FindVariableFeatures and expression values scaled with ScaleData. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on the RNA assay, followed by UMAP embedding using the top 30 principal components.

In a recent development, local perturbation signatures were calculated using CalcPerturbSig from Seurat, subtracting the average expression of the k = 20 nearest non-targeting neighbour cells in PCA space (30 dimensions) to remove technical variation, producing a perturbation assay. The perturbation assay was centred, projected into PCA space using variable features from the RNA assay and visualized by UMAP. Mixscape83 was run on the scaled perturbation assay using RunMixscape with a minimum of five differentially expressed genes, ten iterations and perturbation type set to knockdown. This classified cells as knockdown, escaped or non-targeting based on posterior probability of perturbation. Escaped cells were excluded from all downstream analyses. Knockdown classification rates were computed per perturbation as the proportion of cells assigned knockdown status. Linkage disequilibrium analysis was performed on knockdown and non-targeting control cells using MixscapeLDA on the PRTB assay (ten principal components, log2[fold change] threshold 0.25) and a UMAP was computed on the top linear discriminant analysis dimensions for visualization of perturbation-specific clustering.

Sources indicate that differential expression between KD and non-targeting control cells was performed per perturbation using DESeq2 (v.1.52.0). Cells were assigned randomly to three pseudo-replicates within each perturbation and non-targeting control group, and raw counts were aggregated. Genes with fewer than ten total counts across pseudo-replicates were excluded. Differential expression was tested using a negative binomial model with perturbation condition as the independent variable. Results were filtered at FDR < 0.05.

It has been revealed that pre-ranked GSEA was performed per perturbation using fgsea (v.1.38.0) with genes ranked by log2[fold change] from DESeq2. Gene sets from MSigDB Hallmark and Gene Ontology Biological Process collections were obtained using the msigdbr (v.26.1.1) package (Homo sapiens). Minimum and maximum gene set sizes were set to 10 and 500, respectively, with 1,000 permutations. P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg method across perturbations.

Recent findings suggest that pairwise cosine similarity was computed between the log2[fold change] vectors of all perturbations across the union of tested genes. Missing values were replaced with zero. Perturbations were clustered hierarchically on the resulting similarity matrix and visualized as a heatmap using pheatmap (v.1.0.13).

cNMF26,84 was applied to the raw count matrix of Mixscape-classified knockdown and non-targeting control cells. Counts were exported as an AnnData h5ad file and processed using the cNMF Python package (v.1.7.1). Genes expressed in fewer than five cells and all-zero genes were removed before factorization. Factorization was performed over k = 5–10 components with 100 iterations per k value and random seed 42. The optimal k = 8 was selected based on stability and reconstruction error, with a local-density threshold of 0.01 applied during consensus clustering; 99 of 800 (12%) outlier spectra were removed. Six of eight programmes were retained based on coherent gene set enrichment; two programmes dominated by unannotated loci and lacking enrichment were excluded. cNMF usage scores were imported back into R and added to the Seurat object metadata. Programme identity was assigned by over-representation analysis of the top 100 programme-specific genes against MSigDB Hallmark and Gene Ontology Biological Process gene sets using enricher from clusterProfiler (v.4.20.0).

In a recent development, transcription factor motif enrichment per cNMF programme was assessed by over-representation analysis of top 100 programme genes against Gene Transcription Regulation Database transcription factor target-gene sets from MSigDB C3. Transcription factor activity was estimated using the univariate linear model method implemented in decoupleR (v.2.17.0), with the DoRothEA regulon85 (confidence levels A–C) as the prior network. cNMF gene specificity score vectors (genes × programmes) were used as input. Transcription factors with the highest variance across programmes were retained for visualization.

FMC module scores were computed using AddModuleScore in Seurat on a curated list of FMC marker genes as described above. Stimulated SMC up- and down-regulated gene sets were derived from FindAllMarkers differential expression between stimulated (Zim3_3d3d) and control (Zim3_ctrl) conditions, filtered at FDR < 0.05 and |log2[fold change]| > 0.25. A signed stimulation score was computed as the difference between up- and down-regulated module scores. Spearman correlations between module scores and cNMF programme usage were computed using cor.test. Per perturbation mean scores were compared using the Wilcoxon rank sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. The Spearman correlation between each perturbation’s full log2[fold change] profile and the signed stimulated SMC log2[fold change] vector was computed across shared genes.

According to recent reports, RRA86 was applied across all perturbation DESeq2 gene rankings using the RobustRankAggreg (v.1.2.1) R package, separately for upregulated and down-regulated genes ranked by adjusted P value. Genes passing FDR < 0.05 after Benjamini–Hochberg correction of RRA scores were retained as the convergent programme. Each gene was assigned a direction based on the RRA result with the lower score. The top 30 convergent genes by number of perturbations in which they reached significance were selected for visualization. A convergent programme score was computed per cell as the difference between up and down module scores using AddModuleScore. Pathway enrichment of convergent up and down-regulated genes was performed using enricher against MSigDB Hallmark and GO Biological Process gene sets.

Recent findings suggest that bulk in situ Hi-C libraries for 15 different coronary artery samples across a multi-ethnic cohort were generated with the Arima Hi-C kit, according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Specifically, one Hi-C library was created from each biological sample, with an input of approximately 800,000 cells each. Restriction enzymes cutting at ^GATC and G^ANTC were used in library construction, and approximately 600 million reads were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 4000 per library.

Sources indicate that hi-C reads were processed with the nf-core Hi-C pipeline (v.2.0.0)87 and downstream maps were analysed at 5-kb resolution. Resolution assessment, library quality metrics, loop-caller benchmarking, inherent normalization and visualization procedures88,89 are described in Supplementary Figs. 5–7. Phased contact matrices using sample-specific genotypes were processed using Axiotl’s Turnkey platform (tinker.axiotl.com), which leverages Hi-C-Pro v.3.1.0 and cloud compute.

According to recent reports, we called cohort-specific 3D structures using the AQuA Tools framework90 for 3D genomics. Sample-wise chromatin structures were called in BEDPE format using extract_bedpe. We used union_bedpe to stack and merge BEDPE coordinates coming from various samples into one BEDPE file that contained the union set coordinates of all possible Hi-C connections in the cohort. This allowed for resolving overlapping interactions and outputting a common scaffold. To assign membership (as unique identifiers to column 7) to the stacked loops based on shared overlap of BEDPE anchors, we used cluster_bedpe. This resulting file became the mosaic for the cohort. To assess their functional and disease relevance, we intersected two-dimensional mosaic coordinates with one-dimensional genomic features including genes and snATAC peaks harbouring CAD GWAS variants. Against the mosaic BEDPE, contact values for each sample were queried in inherent and counts per million (CPM) numeric spaces using query_bedpe. All downstream analyses were performed in R.

Sources indicate that all experiments were performed on primary HCASMC between passages 4 and 7. Antibodies used for ChIP–qPCR were all pre-validated according to ChIP–seq guidelines. Purified rabbit monoclonal antibody against human CTCF (Abcam, ab128873; clone EPR7314(B)). Cell lines with various genotypes of rs4887091 were used. Approximately 2 × 106 HCASMC for each line were fixed with 1% formaldehyde and quenched by glycine. The cells were washed three times with PBS and then harvested in ChIP lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8, 5 mM EDTA, 0.5% SDS). Crosslinked chromatin was sheared for 2 × 1 min by sonication (Branson SFX250 Sonifier) before extensive centrifugation. Four volumes of ChIP dilution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X-100) was added to the supernatant. The resulting lysate was then incubated with Dynabeads Protein G (Thermo Scientific, 10009D) and antibodies at 4 °C overnight. Beads were washed once with buffer 1 (20 mM Tris pH 8, 2 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), once with buffer 2 (10 mM Tris pH 8, 1 mM EDTA, 500 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), once with buffer 3 (10 mM Tris pH 8, 1 mM EDTA, 250 mM LiCl, 1% NP40, 1% sodium deoxycholate monohydrate) and twice with TE buffer. DNA was eluted by ChIP elution buffer (0.1 M NaHCO3, 1% SDS, 20 μg ml−1 proteinase K). The elution was incubated at 65 °C overnight, and DNA was extracted with a DNA purification kit (Zymo, D4013). The purified DNA from various lines were analysed by qPCR using the ABI ViiA 7, with the same primer applied to each SNP. Assays were repeated at least three times. Data are average values ± s.d. of representative experiments.

In a recent development, CAD-associated variants were represented as 1-bp genomic intervals (hg38) and intersected with HCASMC CTCF ChIP–seq peak intervals. Observed overlap was defined as the number of CAD variants overlapping at least one CTCF peak. To estimate overlap expected by chance while preserving genomic structure, we performed chromosome-wise circular permutation of CTCF peak coordinates. For each chromosome, peak start coordinates were shifted by a random offset uniformly sampled from \([1,L-1]\), where L is chromosome length, with wraparound at chromosome boundaries. Peak widths and chromosome assignments were preserved. For each of B = 1,000 permutations, we recalculated the number of CAD variants overlapping permuted CTCF peaks to generate an empirical null distribution.

Empirical one-sided P values were computed as.

For parametric approximation, we set \({p}_{0}\) to the null mean overlap probability (mean(null overlaps)/N) and computed the exact one-sided binomial probability of observing \(\ge \)k overlaps among N variants.

According to recent reports, enriched and input DNA were quantified by SYBR Green qPCR on ViiA 7. In addition to SYBR Green primers, we also used TaqMan genotyping probe (ThermoFisher, AN7EEGX, lot no. P260615-009) to directly amplify the different alleles of the DNA in heterozygous lines. Relative CTCF enrichment for target (rs4887091) and control loci was calculated as percent input. Target allele-specific binding effects were confirmed by benchmarking enrichment profiles against the expected quantitative gradients of the in-house validated allelic controls.

Sources indicate that to identify endogenous allelic controls across the four cell lines, CTCF ChIP–seq peaks were intersected with corresponding whole-genome sequencing VCF files. SNPs exhibiting complete genotypic gradients (homozygous reference, heterozygous, homozygous alternative) were scored for CTCF motif perturbation using the JASPAR matrix (MA0139.2). Allelic positive controls were defined by severe motif disruption (\(\Delta \text{Score}\ge 6.0\), max score \( > 8.0\)), whereas negative controls exhibited preserved motif integrity (\(\Delta \text{Score}\le 0.2\), both scores \( > 8.0\)).

Sources indicate that to prevent cross-cell-line amplification bias, SYBR Green qPCR primers (75–150 bp amplicons) were designed using Primer3 v.2.6.1. An in silico masking pipeline strictly discarded any candidate primer pairs whose binding sites overlapped with endogenous variants in the merged four-cell-line VCF, ensuring 100% conserved annealing kinetics across all biological samples.

Hi-ChIP was adapted from previously published protocols with some modifications91,92. Briefly, at least 1 million healthy HCASMCs (Thermo Scientific, C-017-5C, lot no. 1689414) and healthy HCAECs (ATCC, PCS-100-020, lot no. 62382179) were crosslinked with 1% formaldehyde. The initial Hi-C portion followed the Arima Hi-C protocol described in the Arima High Coverage Hi-C Kit (Arima Genomics, A410110). For the immunoprecipitation step, sheared chromatin after the Hi-C portion of the protocol was immunoprecipitated with 5 μg of H3K27ac antibody (Abcam, ab4729) with 50 μl of protein G Dynabeads (Invitrogen 10004D) and allowed to incubate overnight at 4 °C. The protein G Dynabeads were washed and the immunoprecipitated DNA was de-crosslinked at 67 °C for 2 h and eluted (50 mM sodium bicarbonate, 1% SDS). Subsequently, Dynabeads MyOne Streptavidin C1 beads (Invitrogen, 65002) were used to enrich ligated junctions as per Hi-C protocol. Library preparation was performed using the NEB Ultra II library preparation kit (NEB, E7645L), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Twelve PCR cycles were performed using indexed primers and subsequently DNA fragments between 300 bp and 500 bp were size selected using the Omega MagBind NGS clean up Magnetic beads (Omega, M1378). The libraries were sequenced by paired-end sequencing with at least 300 million read pairs at 2 × 151-bp read length on Illumina HiSeq 4000 platforms. Raw paired-end reads in Fastq format for respective samples were processed using the Hi-CuP pipeline93 (v.0.7.4). The hg38 human genome was used as reference to generate the Hi-CuP Digest file using two restriction motifs GATC and GANTC using the hicup_digester command for running the Hi-CuP pipeline. Paired contacts were extracted from aligned filtered bam files using Samtools (v.1.13) and used as input for the pre function in the Juicer package to generate hic files94. Paired interaction counts at 5 kb resolution were extracted from the matrix, and high-confidence chromatin loops were identified using the FitHiChIP tool (v.11.0) as described previously using default parameters95. Using HCASMC and HCAEC ChIP–seq peak files as input, and initial paired interaction files, high-confidence peak-to-all interactions with a 5-kb bin size were processed using the bash FitHiChIP_HiCPro.sh script (https://ay-lab.github.io/FitHiChIP/). High-confidence chromatin interactions were sorted and indexed in bed format and converted to long-range format for visualization on the WashU browser. The overlay of Hi-ChIP, ChIP–seq and GWAS data was plotted using the locuszoomr package (v.0.3.5) and R (v.4.3.1).

ChIP–seq was performed as described previously with minor optimizations96. Briefly, 1 million HCASMCs and HCAECs from the same lot used for Hi-ChIP experiments were crosslinked with 1% formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature and quenched with glycine (125 mM) for 5 min. The cells were rinsed twice with cold 1× PBS and sonicated in nuclei lysis buffer (50 mM HEPES–KOH, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X, 0.1% sodium deoxycholate, 1% SDS, Takara, 1× protease inhibitor) using the Bioruptor sonicator to obtain chromatin fragments between 200 bp and 500 bp. The fragmented chromatin was immunoprecipitated overnight at 4 °C, with 5 μg of H3K27ac antibody (Abcam, ab4729) and 50 μl of protein G beads (Invitrogen, 10004D). Subsequently, the beads were washed and immunoprecipitated DNA was de-crosslinked and eluted in elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, and 10 mM EDTA). Eluted ChIP fragments were isolated using phenol–chloroform extraction method, and DNA was purified by ethanol precipitation. Library preparation was performed on the eluted ChIP DNA using the NEB Ultra II library preparation kit, according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Ten PCR cycles were performed using indexed primers and the library of DNA fragments with sizes between 300 bp and 500 bp was selected using the Omega MagBind NGS clean up Magnetic beads (Omega, M1378). The libraries were sent for paired-end sequencing, with at least 50 million read pairs at 2 × 151-bp read length on the Illumina HiSeq 4000 platform. Paired-end sequencing reads were aligned to human genome (hg38) using BWA mem v.0.7.5 (ref. 97), and reads were deduplicated using Picard v.3.4.0 MarkDuplicates. Aligned mapped reads in BAM file were used as input for peak-calling using Dfilter98 to identify significant H3K27ac peaks using the following setting: -ks = 60, -bs = 100, -Ipvalue = 8. Bigwig tracks were normalized for sequencing depths and the sum of normalized binned tag-count represents the peak height.

Sources indicate that healthy HCASMCs (Thermo Scientific, C-017-5C, lot no. 1689414) were cultured in human vascular smooth muscle basal medium (Gibco, M231500), in Smooth Muscle Growth Supplement (Gibco, S00725) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. Healthy HCAECs (ATCC, PCS-100-020, lot no. 62382179) were cultured in Endothelial Cell Growth medium MV2 (PromoCell, C-22022).

The Lentiguide-Puro plasmid was obtained as a gift from F. Zhang (Addgene, 52963, LentiGuide-Puro) in which the non-targeting control sgRNAs and sgRNAs targeting the TSS and regulatory enhancer were annealed and ligated into the Esp3I cut-site of the Lentiguide-Puro vector using T4 Ligase (NEB, M0202) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Ligation products were transformed into One Shot Stbl3 Chemically competent Escherichia coli (Invitrogen, C737303) and plasmids of positive clones were isolated using FavorPrep Plasmid DNA Extract Kit (Favorgen, FAPDE001-1). The CRISPR interference expression vector for Lenti-dCas9-KRAB-blast (Addgene, 89567) was a gift from G. Hon. For lentivirus production, HEK293T cells were cultured in DMEM + 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) until 70% confluency before transfection. Then, 10 μg of individual plasmids, 7.5 μg of pMDLg/RRE, 2.5 μg of pRSV-Rev and 2.5 μg of pMD2.G lentivirus packaging plasmids were co-transfected with 50 μl of polyethylenimine diluted in 3 ml of Opti-MEM I Reduced Serum Medium (ThermoFisher Scientific, 31985070). Medium was refreshed overnight with reduced 5% FBS in DMEM medium, and the expended medium was collected twice after 24 h and 48 h, respectively. Pooled supernatant was filtered through a polyethersulfone 0.45 μm filter and viral particles were concentrated using Viro-PEG Lentivirus Concentrator (Ozbiosciences, LVG100) as per the manufacturer’s instructions.

In a recent development, at least two independent sgRNAs targeting a single regulatory element were tested against the non-targeting control. sgRNA targeting the TSS was used as positive control. Healthy HCASMCs (Thermo Scientific, C-017-5C, lot no. 1689414) and HCAECs (ATCC, PCS-100-020, lot no. 62382179) were both co-transduced in 5 μg ml−1 polybrene with lentiviral particles packaged from Lenti-dCas9-KRAB-blast (Addgene, 89567)99, and individual sgRNAs were cloned into Lentiguide-Puro backbone (Addgene, 52963)100 at a multiplicity of infection of 3. Respective HCASMC and HCAEC growth media were refreshed after 24 h of infection, and co-selection with 10 μg ml−1 blasticidin (Gibco, A1113903) and 1 μg ml−1 puromycin (Gibco, A1113803) was performed 72 h following infection. Selected cells were allowed to recover and expanded for 2 weeks before RNA isolation using Trizol Reagent (Gibco, 15596026) and Direct-Zol RNA miniprep (Zymo Research, R2052) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA conversion was performed with at least 200 ng RNA using HiScript III RT SuperMix (Vazyme Biotech, R323-01), and reverse transcription-PCR was performed using gene-specific primers to assess for gene expression.

It has been revealed that cell kinetic proliferation live-cell imaging was performed using the HoloMonitor M4 system (Phase Holographic Imaging, PHI AB) using the Cell Kinetic Proliferation assay protocol as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Non-targeting controls and AMOTL2 dCas9-KRAB CRISPRi knockdown HCASMCs were seeded and cultured in vascular smooth muscle cell medium, in smooth muscle growth supplement, at a confluence of 15,000 cells cm−2 in a 24-well vessel (VWR, 734-2325) (n = 8). The 24-well HoloLid (PHI AB, 71130) was used to enhance the visualization and tracking of cells. At least five capture areas were taken per well, and time-lapse imaging at every 30-min time interval was taken across wells over 72 h. Cellular segmentation was performed using the HoloMonitor App Suite (v.3.5.2.446). Cellular confluence was captured and normalized to baseline at 0 h.

Industry observers note that total RNA was extracted using Trizol Reagent (ThermoFisher, 15596026) and Direct-Zol RNA miniprep Kit (Zymo Research, R2050). At least three independent replicates were used for RNA library preparations. RNA quality and yield was assessed using Agilent RNA 6000 pico kit (Agilent, 5067-1513) for quality. Bulk RNA-seq library preparations were prepared using VAHTS Universal V10 RNA-seq Library Prep Kit for Illumina (Vazyme, NR606-01) with Ribodepletion, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA libraries were prepared using Illumina RNA Truseq indexes and quantified using Agilent Tapestation. Sequencing was performed on the NovaSeq X Plus (PE150) by NovogeneAIT Singapore, yielding 50 million raw pair-end reads. Raw Fastq files were trimmed using the trim-galore tool (v.0.65) from Babraham Bioinformatics to sequence length of 50. Paired-end reads were mapped and aligned to the human reference genome GRCh38–hg38 using STAR aligner (v.2.7.0) as per default settings and using gene annotations from GENCODE v.38. Aligned gene counts were mapped using HTSeq-count v.2.1.2 and normalized to TPM by sequencing depth and by gene length. Differential gene-expression analysis was performed using EdgeR (v.3.42.4). Contrasts were compared between non-targeting control and AMOTL2 TSS knockdown cells. A negative binomial generalized log-linear model was used to model gene counts using the glmFit function. |log[fold change]| >0.5 and FDR < 0.05 cut-offs were used to identify significantly differentially expressed genes following multiple testing correction. Figures were generated with R v.3.5.1.

HCASMCs were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (ThermoFisher, 5090495) for 15 min at room temperature, then washed with 3× PBS for 5 min at room temperature. Cells were permeabilized with PBS with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 15 min, followed by blocking in 5% normal goat serum in PBS (blocking buffer) for 1 h at room temperature. Primary anti-Calponin (1:100) (ProteinTech, 13938-1-AP), and primary anti-α-smooth muscle actin antibody (1:100) (Sigma-Aldrich, A5228) were diluted in blocking buffer and added to permeabilized cells overnight at 4 °C. After washing with PBS three times for 5 min, cells were incubated with Alexa fluor-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:1,000) (Goat anti-mouse 594, ThermoFisher, A-11032; goat anti-rabbit 488, ThermoFisher, A-11008) and 1 μg ml−1 DAPI for 1 h at room temperature. Stained cells were washed three times for 5 min each with PBS, and images were acquired under the same laser exposure and magnification using a fluorescence microscope (EVOS M7000).

N.O.S. and I.M.H. conceived the study. J.M.A., T.Y. and A.B. isolated nuclei and performed 10x Multi-ome experiments on human coronary arteries. P.C.L., X.L., Y.Z., C.W.-R., C.L.M. and B.L. performed QTL analyses. M.U.S., W.-L.Q., A.T., R.A. and J.M.E. performed enhancer–gene linkage analyses. J.M.A., I.E., T.Y., M.C., R.G.G., K.J.L., Y.-H.H., R.S., C.-M.L., B.A. and N.O.S. designed and contributed to analysis of the Hi-C data. C.J.M.L., R.G., C.A.-N., W.Q.S. and R.S.-Y.F. performed in vitro Hi-ChIP, H3K27ac and CRISPR interference experiments. Q.Z., T.N., D.Y.L., M.R. and T.Q. performed in vitro CRISPR interference validation and CTCF experiments. P.C.L., H.C.P.P., Y.W., J.O., R.E.W. and A.A. performed EMSA experiments. J.M.A., T.Y., C.J.M.L., E.Y., W.-L.L., J.C., D.R.L., S.H., S.M. and S.J. designed, performed and contributed to the Perturb–seq experiments. J.M.A., P.C.L., C.J.M.L., R.S.W., S.K., D.K., C.K., P.C., I.M.H., R.M.G., S.M.H., R.K., P.S., H.Y.C., B.L., S.M., S.J., T.Q. and N.O.S. provided guidance on GWAS mapping, data interpretation and cell-specific analyses. C.J.K. analysed genotyping data. J.M.A., S.J. and N.O.S. supervised the work. J.M.A., P.C.L., T.Q. and N.O.S. drafted the manuscript with assistance from all authors. N.O.S. is responsible for all aspects of this manuscript including experimental design, data analysis and manuscript production. All authors edited and approved the final version of the manuscript.

Recent findings suggest that (a) Gene set scores for marker genes (adjusted P value < 0.05 and log2FC > 0.58) in each cell type. P values were calculated using one-sided Fisher’s exact tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. (b) Dot plot of marker gene set score from (a) grouped by cell type. (c) Dot plot of canonical RNA marker genes by cell type, colored by average expression; dot size indicates percent of cells in the cluster which express the gene. (d) Multiome peaks grouped by distal, exonic, intronic, and promoter from macs2 peak calls split by cell type. (e) Differentially accessible marker peaks heatmap by cell type; statistically significant peaks (FDR < 0.1 and log2FC > 0.5).

Each point represents enhancer-gene predictions by scE2GMultiome in one cell cluster (N = 11). All properties were computed on binarized predictions omitting promoter elements. (a) Average number of unique ATAC fragments per cell by number of cells per cluster. (b) Number of enhancer-gene links by number of unique ATAC fragments per cluster. (c) Mean enhancer width by number of unique enhancer elements regulating at least one distal gene. (d) Mean distance between enhancer element and target gene transcription start site. (e) Mean number of enhancers per gene by mean number of genes per enhancer. (f) Number of genes with at least one non-promoter enhancer by number of unique ATAC fragments. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that defenders Nuno Tavares and Josip Sutalo hurt their hamstrings at Napoli, leaving unbeaten Serie A leaders Lazio short in defence.
  • It has been revealed that lazio’s defence has suffered a double blow.
  • According to recent reports, exact recovery times will only be set once all clinical tests are complete.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that defenders Nuno Tavares and Josip Sutalo hurt their hamstrings at Napoli, leaving unbeaten Serie A leaders Lazio short in defence. The setback hits Gattuso's back line just as Juventus return from the break chasing the leaders.

It has been revealed that lazio’s defence has suffered a double blow. Nuno Tavares and Josip Sutalo were both injured in the 1-1 draw at Napoli. The timing is awkward for the leaders, who resume their league campaign against Lecce on 21 November.

According to recent reports, exact recovery times will only be set once all clinical tests are complete. The early estimate is about 20 days for each player, Sky Sport Italia reported. On that timeline, both miss the home game against Lecce and could return for the trip to Torino on 28 November.

Recent findings suggest that not every report is that hopeful. Football Italia reported that the pair should miss both the Lecce and Torino games. Under that scenario, they hope to be available again in the first week of December. The match against Atalanta on 6 December is also in doubt.

It has been revealed that tavares has been a real attacking outlet this season. He has one goal and four assists in 11 Serie A games. He also has a long record of muscle injuries. Sutalo has made eight league appearances since joining on loan from Ajax on 22 August.

Lazio must now turn to their alternatives. Alfonso Pedraza, who joined from Villarreal in the summer, is the leading option at left-back. He has played 322 minutes across the league and Coppa Italia. Diogo Leite and Doekhi are competing to replace Sutalo in the middle.

The stand-ins inherit a strong record. Lazio have scored 25 goals and conceded 9 so far. Keeping that defensive record with a reshuffled back line is now Gattuso’s task.

Juventus know Lazio’s quality first-hand. Gattuso’s side won 3-0 in Turin earlier this season. That result still weighs on the table. Five wins, three draws and three defeats make up the Juventus record from their opening games.

Grande chiusura di Sutalo, fondamentale.

— S.S.Lazio (@OfficialSSLazio) November 8, 2026.

Two missing defenders will not close the gap on their own. They do, however, give Juventus a window in which the leaders are weaker than usual. Any dropped points by Lazio over the coming rounds would only count if Juventus take care of their own fixtures.

In a recent development, those fixtures follow Lazio’s closely. Como v Juventus is scheduled for Sunday 29 November at 20:45, the day after Lazio’s game against Torino. Further ahead, Lazio’s aim is to have both defenders fit for the Rome derby on 13 December.

Industry observers note that as Ruben Amorim explained in his post-match press conference after Olympiacos 2-4 Milan, Ramos was substituted at the break due to a physical problem. The Portuguese striker suffered a severe blow to his shin that prevented him from continuing the match.

Thuram and Locatelli absences leave Juventus midfield thin for four games in 12 days

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (465 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Juvefc

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Khéphren Thuram and Manuel Locatelli will miss the rest of 2026 after knee surgery, leaving Spalletti short in midfield for a congested run of fixtures.
  • It has been revealed that two senior midfielders will be missing as Juventus head into a congested run of fixtures.
  • Thuram underwent chondroplasty to treat patellar chondropathy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Khéphren Thuram and Manuel Locatelli will miss the rest of 2026 after knee surgery, leaving Spalletti short in midfield for a congested run of fixtures. Højbjerg has emerged as the name Juventus want to cover the gap in January.

It has been revealed that two senior midfielders will be missing as Juventus head into a congested run of fixtures. Thuram should be back with the group in January, and Locatelli only in the spring, Sport Mediaset reported. Both men are recovering from operations on the right knee.

Thuram underwent chondroplasty to treat patellar chondropathy. Dr Bertrand Sonnery-Cottet carried out the procedure at the Hôpital Privé Jean Mermoz in Lyon. Locatelli had his external meniscus sutured, also in Lyon, after spraining the knee against Milan. He was due to start rehabilitation the day after the operation.

Spalletti now has to rely on Douglas Luiz, Koopmeiners and newly introduced signing Pape Matar Sarr in the middle. The run opens with Venezia at 12:30 on 22 November. Omonia visit the Allianz Stadium at 21:00 on 26 November. The trip to Como follows at 20:45 on 29 November. The sequence closes with a Coppa Italia last-16 tie against Sassuolo.

Recent findings suggest that como present a sharp test. Fàbregas’s side have 23 points. They play a European fixture on 24 November, five days before they host Juventus.

The table leaves little room for slips. Juventus have 18 points from five wins, three draws and three defeats. They are 11 points behind leaders Lazio and six points off the Champions League places.

Sarr arrived on 1 September on loan from Tottenham until 30 June 2027. Juventus paid a €2.5 million fee plus €0.3 million in additional costs. The deal includes a €27.5 million permanent transfer, spread over three financial years. That becomes compulsory if certain conditions are met during 2026/27. The club describes him as a physically strong box-to-box midfielder. He has more than 100 Premier League appearances and won the 2024/25 Europa League with Spurs.

There is some relief elsewhere in the squad. Nico Gonzalez, Conceição and Cambiaso could all be available for Venezia. Yildiz hopes to return around December.

The absences make a January move for a midfielder more likely. Juventus have three targets for the window: a centre-forward, a defensive midfielder and a left-back. Pierre-Emile Højbjerg is the name for midfield, with Sørloth and Miranda also on the list, QS reported.

Industry observers note that the profile is clear. Juventus want an experienced midfielder to bridge the gap until Thuram returns and Locatelli follows later. These remain media reports rather than a club statement.

Until then, the existing group must carry the load. The Coppa Italia tie with Sassuolo is set for the Allianz Stadium in Turin on Thursday 3 December at 21:00.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 27 Nov 2026 11:24, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 11:44.

The stuttering champions and the challengers-in-crisis face off in Sunday's Premier League main event, which sees Arsenal and Manchester City draw swords at the Emirates Stadium.

The Gunners hold a six-point advantage over Enzo Maresca's men at the summit of the Premier League table, leading some to deduce that another success for the holders could already expel the Sky Blues from the title race.

Out of sight in first place, boasting the best defence in the top flight and taking 16 points from the last 18 on offer in the Premier League, Arsenal have lived up to their early-season expectations as the overwhelming favourites to retain their crown.

Yet, the Emirates faithful cannot shake the feeling that there is still something missing in Mikel Arteta's ranks, after Arsenal's second-half shortcomings were exposed in back-to-back draws with Newcastle United and Borussia Dortmund.

Both stalemates saw the Gunners fail to hold onto and build on one-goal advantages in the first half, before their foes came out all guns blazing after the restart and capitalised on Arsenal's alarming lack of a ruthless attacking touch.

Only four of Arsenal's 30 shots on goal in the Champions League were on target, as their 12-game winning run in home league phase/group stage fixtures came to an end, and their 17 Premier League goals scored so far ranks as the worst among all top-six teams.

However, the holders are five from five at the Emirates Stadium in the top flight - scoring 10 times and conceding just twice in the process - and they are yet to draw a blank at home in any tournament this term.

Interestingly, Arsenal's 10 home goals matches Man City's 10 away strikes in the 2026-27 Premier League season, while only Brighton & Hove Albion (26) can better the visitors' overall total of 22.

Such statistics will come as little consolation to travelling fans amid the Sky Blues' sorry slump, though, as Enzo Maresca's men have collected just one point from the last 12 on offer in the top flight after a perfect seven from seven to start the campaign.

The Citizens at least managed to snap their three-game losing sequence in last week's 1-1 draw at home to Fulham - not that such a feat was worth celebrating, though - before they also had to settle for a point in their midweek Champions League clash with Napoli.

Maresca and former Man City players have disagreed over whether the club's guilty verdict and appeal uncertainty over their 115 charges is impacting on-field performances, but the manager himself now finds himself under fire for questionable tactical calls and team selections over the autumnal period.

There is no suggestion that the former Chelsea boss is under any immediate sack pressure, though, despite presiding over a 122-year worst; City are just the second team in English Football League history to win their first seven matches of a season but fail to triumph in any of their next four, after the 1904-05 Sheffield Wednesday crop.

Furthermore, the Sky Blues were swatted aside in August's 3-0 Community Shield defeat to Arsenal, who have only lost two of their last nine head-to-heads against Man City and are unbeaten in their last three meetings on Emirates soil.

Arsenal form (all competitions):.

Manchester City Premier League form:.

Manchester City form (all competitions):.

Fears of a serious shoulder injury to Arsenal number one David Raya have been allayed by Arteta, and at the time of writing, the Spain international has not been officially ruled out of the visit of Man City.

Arsenal will also welcome teenage wonderkid Max Dowman back from a three-game domestic suspension, but Martin Zubimendi (hamstring) and Bukayo Saka (quad) will not be back until just before Christmas at the earliest.

After Christos Tzolis's underwhelming midweek display, expect Eberechi Eze to return to the forward line, where Arteta has a critical choice to make between Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz after the former's thunderous finish in midweek.

Meanwhile, captain Martin Odegaard has another Premier League record in his sights; if he sets up two goals here, he will equal the record for the most assists by a Norwegian player in the competition - his 38 is marginally inferior to Morten Gamst Pedersen's 40.

Meanwhile, Man City are expected to head south with a fully-fit squad barring former Arsenal transfer target Antoine Semenyo, who is a few weeks away from returning from a knee injury.

Snubbed from the starting XI against Fulham before saving City's skin against Napoli, Rayan Cherki has surely done enough to hold his spot at the Emirates, while Jeremy Doku and Iliman Ndiaye also have cases to come back in after providing assists off the bench last time out.

Goalless in his last three Premier League matches, Erling Haaland could equal his own personal worst for an English top-flight goal drought, having never gone longer than four Premier League games without finding the back of the net.

Arsenal possible starting lineup:.

Raya; Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori; Guimaraes, Rice; Madueke, Odegaard, Eze; Havertz.

Manchester City possible starting lineup:.

Donnarumma; Nunes, Guehi, Dias, O'Reilly; Anderson, Fernandez; Ndiaye, Cherki, Doku; Haaland.

The defensive numbers make for dreadful reading for Man City, who have let in seven goals across their last three away games and are without a clean sheet in 10 fixtures in total.

A profligate Arsenal side may not be the best-placed to capitalise, as only one of their last five wins has been by more than a one-goal margin, but the champions should still demonstrate why they are champions and deal another blow to Man City's already-fading title hopes.
